Carlsberg (CARL.B-DK) · Investment memo

Carlsberg: a predictable 8%-a-year EPS compounder priced at the bottom of its own multiple range, whose return depends on a re-rating that the sector half decides

3 November 2026. Share price DKK 934.2 at the close on 29 October 2026, the day of the Q3 trading statement (down 3.0% on the day); market value about DKK 124bn. The Financial Analyst's model priced the shares at DKK 960.6 (28 October), so this memo quotes returns from DKK 960.6; from today's DKK 934.2, every return is about three percentage points higher.

Definitions. EBIT is operating profit on Carlsberg's own performance measures; EPS is the company's adjusted EPS; leverage is net interest-bearing debt to EBITDA. Every multiple in this memo uses EPS corrected for minority interests. The full definitions, the model's minorities correction and two cautions about the source files are in the end notes.

#0 Summary of key insights, implications and conclusions

Carlsberg is a self-help and capital-return compounder with no demand growth, priced at the 8th percentile of its own ten-year multiple. Management controls most of what the next 18 months of profit depend on: the last Britvic synergies, the new Kazakhstan plant that replaces loss-making toll-filling, a balance sheet that reaches the 2.5x leverage target a year early, and a buyback restart that consensus has not modelled. Management does not control the three things the share price answers to: the Chinese consumer, the 2027 input-cost round, and a European beverage multiple set by sector flows.

The result is a case whose earnings are unusually predictable and whose return depends unusually heavily on the multiple. EPS should grow about 8% a year, and FY2027 EPS should land within about 5% either way of the base case. Without any re-rating, the shares offer about 12-13% a year in steady state (about 8% EPS growth plus a 3.4% dividend yield); the return over the model's 18-month column is higher, because the forward-earnings window rolls onto FY2029. At the guideline fair multiple of 15.27x, the shares offer about 33% annualised over the same 18-month column.

The timing runs the wrong way round for an investor buying now. February to April 2027 is likely to bring disappointment through the composition of earnings; August 2027 is likely to bring reassurance through delivery and the buyback.

The probability-weighted 18-month return is about +22% including dividends, so the case is attractive for a 12-24 month holder at either entry point, and the spring of 2027 is the better window to buy.

The eight insights that matter most

1Key message
Carlsberg's earnings engine is self-help, and the self-help is front-loaded. Named levers (Britvic synergies, Kazakhstan in-housing and restructurings) supply more than half of EBIT growth in FY2026 and FY2027, but only about one-sixth in FY2028. From FY2028, 5% EBIT growth has to come from price running ahead of cost, with no named programme behind it. No sell-side house quantifies this fade of self-help. The fade is why the forecasts hold EBIT growth at 5% rather than at management's floated "high-single-digit compounding", and why the three-year leg of the case carries less weight than the 18-month leg.
2Key message
The hybrid bond moved part of Carlsberg's financing cost below net income; it did not remove the cost. The cut in net finance cost guidance from DKK 2.2bn to DKK 1.8bn reads as a saving, but about DKK 150-250m of the cut is reclassification under IFRS 18. The hybrid's coupon (DKK 620m gross, DKK 477m after tax, about DKK 3.6 a share) now sits below net income, where several brokers do not deduct it. The combined cost of debt plus hybrid falls only from about DKK 2.34bn in 2026 to DKK 2.27bn in 2027, so from 2028 the balance sheet adds to EPS through the falling share count, not through lower interest. The hybrid is the mechanic the market most mis-models, and the first clean IFRS 18 full-year results, on 9 February 2027, will force brokers to correct it.
3Key message
Carlsberg's minority interests are proportionally the largest among European brewers, and they sit in its most profitable subsidiaries. Minorities took DKK 1,023m in FY2025, 14.65% of consolidated profit, against 11.8% at Heineken. Outside shareholders own 40% of Chongqing Brewery, 39% of Lao Brewery and 49% of Carlsberg Malaysia, and Sapporo's 25% of Southeast Asia adds to the minority share from 2027. Leaving minorities out had inflated the model's EPS by 13-16%; with the correction, the model lands at consensus. The minorities also cut the other way: roughly half of any swing in Chinese profit never reaches Carlsberg's EPS, so the share price reacts to China far more than China's effect on EPS justifies.
4Key message
Consensus FY2027 EPS is right in level and wrong in composition. Consensus FY2027 EPS of DKK 69.25 is close to the model's DKK 70.91 (and to the Analyst's cross-check of DKK 69.97), but consensus reaches it by a different route. Consensus carries too much revenue growth (+3.8% against the model's +3.1%), too little leakage below EBIT, and no buyback. The corrections net to about zero at the EPS line, but they arrive in an unfavourable order: cuts to revenue and to the lines below EBIT come first (to April 2027), and the benefit of a lower share count comes second (from August 2027).
5The buyback is the one dated positive that consensus has not modelled. Leverage reaches about 2.5x at end-2026 if Sapporo's purchase closes in Q4, as management says (about 2.7x if the closing slips). Management has said that reaching 2.5x "will not automatically trigger" a buyback and that a February announcement is unlikely. The base case is a DKK 2bn buyback from August 2027 and DKK 4-5bn a year from 2028. Buybacks of that size retire about 2.5-3.5% of the shares a year and add 2.5-3.5 points of EPS growth that no consensus model carries. Only an Indian listing (draft prospectus filed 27 October; market talk of a December launch; up to USD 700m) could bring the buyback forward.
6Carlsberg's pricing power is nominal, not real. Carlsberg is the market leader in only 24% of its volume by weight and a challenger in 66%. The company passes excise and cost increases through with a lag, has not recently raised prices faster than inflation, and concedes mainstream volume (in the UK and Poland) rather than fight for it. The 2027 cost round (about 160bp of gross margin, with input inflation of about 5.4%) is the test. Carlsberg's policy is to cover more than 80% of input inflation in money and to let the gross-margin percentage slip. Price against cost, not volume, is the largest source of variance in FY2027 EBIT.
7About two-thirds of Carlsberg's multiple is a call on the sector. Nine of the eleven stocks in the dashboard's beverages sector trade below the 10th percentile of their own ten-year multiple range. The October rotation lifted brewers by 9.6-17.4% with no support from estimates: Carlsberg rose 14.1% while its average target price fell 0.2%. Carlsberg then fell 3% on its own volume miss, a day after Heineken rose on its own volume beat. The part Carlsberg does control is its roughly 17% discount to European beverage peers and to AB InBev's 15.6x. The buyback and a Chinese stabilisation can close about half of that discount, which is worth 8-10% on the share price regardless of the sector.
8Key message
The entry point is better after the spring of 2027 than before it, unless an Indian listing lands in December. February 2027 brings a wide initial FY2027 guidance range (2-6% or 3-7%, midpoint 4-5%) against consensus EBIT growth of 5.9%, the hybrid coupon shown below net income, revenue forecasts cut towards 3%, and sell-side breadth at its worst. August 2027 brings the H1 beat, the upward narrowing of guidance and the buyback. For a 12-24 month holder, the most likely outcome is attractive at either entry point; for timing, the spring is the window.

The market has the shape of the story right and three pieces of its arithmetic wrong. The buy-side narrative, as far as brokers' notes and price behaviour reveal it, is "cheap, defensive, multi-beverage, buyback coming, China the risk", and all five parts of that narrative are right. The narrative misses the arithmetic below EBIT that makes 2027 a pinch year, the fade of self-help after 2027, and the true size of 2027 EPS growth. On the model's build, 2027 EPS growth is about 6%, not the 13% a year to 2029 that the most-quoted bull, Bernstein, carries; growth of 13% a year needs both an Indian listing and a DKK 4-5bn buyback every year.

The five judgements that move the value most, with the arithmetic

Each judgement is sized as a plausible miss against the model's base case: FY2027 EBIT of DKK 15.34bn and EPS of DKK 70.91 on about 131m average shares; FY2028 EPS of DKK 76.99 on 127.0m shares; and FY2029 EPS of DKK 83.77. Two conversion rules apply throughout. A DKK 100m change in wholly owned EBIT is worth about DKK 0.59 of EPS (DKK 100m × 0.77 after tax, over 131m shares). The same change in Chinese EBIT is worth only about DKK 0.35, because 40% of Chongqing Brewery belongs to other shareholders.

1. Price against cost in 2027 is the largest operating swing. The base case assumes pure price of about 2.6%, revenue per hectolitre of about +2.1% after soft-drink and Chinese mix, a gross margin flat to 30bp lower, and EBIT growth of 5%. Each 0.5 point of price and mix is worth about DKK 475m of revenue and DKK 300-450m of EBIT (2-3%), because price falls almost entirely to profit.

Downside (about 25% probability): revenue per hectolitre rises only 1.5% while input inflation runs above 5%. EBIT falls about DKK 400m short, EBIT growth drops to about 2.7%, and EPS falls DKK 2.4 to about DKK 68.5 (-3.4%).

Upside (about 20% probability): the whole industry passes aluminium and glass costs through, and price holds at 3%. EBIT gains DKK 350m, and EPS gains DKK 2.0 to about DKK 72.9.

Precedents. For the downside: in 2011, price increases taken to cover costs lost 250bp of volume share in a quarter, and in 2022 gross margin fell 190bp. For the floor: in 2020, 2022-23 and 2025, management flexed operating costs and still grew organic EBIT.

2. China in 2027 moves the share price far more than it moves EPS. China is about 14% of revenue and roughly a fifth of EBIT (about DKK 2.7-2.9bn after the fall in 2026), and the second and third quarters earn about two-thirds of China's profit. The base case assumes Chinese volume of +2% on easy comparatives from Q2 2027 (volume fell 6% in Q2 2026 and 10% in Q3 2026) and Chinese EBIT growth of 3-5% (+DKK 100m).

Downside: a second weak summer, with volume -5% and Chinese EBIT -8%. The swing against the base case is about -DKK 320m of EBIT (-2.1% of group EBIT), but only -DKK 1.1 of EPS (-1.6%) after the 40% minority.

Structural case (low probability): a 20% fall in Chinese profit costs about DKK 580m of EBIT (-4%) and about DKK 2.0 of EPS (-2.9%), and delays the buyback.

The asymmetry to hold onto: Carlsberg's shares have moved 5-15% on Chinese results whose effect on EPS was 1-3%.

3. The buyback's date and size decide FY2028 EPS. The base case is a DKK 2bn buyback from August 2027 and DKK 4bn in 2028, giving average shares of 130.6m in FY2027 and 127.0m in FY2028. The buyback is also the only mechanism by which the balance sheet adds to EPS from 2028, since the interest saved is largely paid out as the hybrid coupon.

Downside, a one-year delay (if Sapporo's closing slips or EBIT growth stalls near 3%): FY2028 average shares stay at about 131.9m, so FY2028 EPS falls to about DKK 74.1 (DKK 77.0 × 127.0 / 131.9), 3.7% below base, and FY2029 EPS ends about 3% below base.

Upside, an Indian listing: DKK 4-5bn of proceeds spent on shares at about DKK 1,000 retires 4-5m shares (3-4%). Net of the new Indian minority (India is about 3-4% of group EBITDA), the listing adds about 2% to FY2028 EPS.

4. Three unguided lines below EBIT (finance costs, minorities and the hybrid) explain the spread in broker forecasts. Nineteen brokers' FY2027 EPS forecasts run from DKK 65.57 to DKK 75.79, although their revenue forecasts sit within 4% of each other. The table sets out the model's choice on each line against the brokers'. The Sapporo minority charge alone is disputed by a factor of four (Bernstein DKK 40m, earlier forecast sets DKK 150m, the model DKK 100m), a difference of DKK 0.8 of EPS between the extremes. February's finance-cost guidance is the near-term test: guidance of DKK 1.8bn or above would take about DKK 1.2 off the model's FY2027 EPS, and guidance of DKK 1.6bn or below would add DKK 1-1.5 to the sell-side's mean.

5. The multiple sets the width of the return range; the earnings do not. At end-2027 the two-year-forward EPS is FY2029's DKK 83.77, so each turn of multiple is worth DKK 84 a share, about 9% of today's price. At 11.3x (the five-year 10th percentile) the shares are worth DKK 947, and at the guideline 15.27x they are worth DKK 1,279; topic 12 tabulates the steps between. On the downside EPS path (FY2029 EPS about DKK 76) at 11.3x, the shares are worth about DKK 860. Dividends add DKK 66 over the period. From DKK 934, the share-price range is therefore about -8% to +37% before dividends, with the most likely outcome at +16% to +24%.
