#1Tailwinds in the operating environment, and the absence of headwinds

Carlsberg's operating environment is a moderate headwind, and the headwind has worsened over the past twelve months. Five external forces work against the company.

  • Beer demand is flat to declining. Beer is about two-thirds of Carlsberg's volume. Global beer volume grows 0.2% a year to 2030; Carlsberg's footprint embeds growth of 0.3% a year, the lowest of the major brewers (Heineken 1.0%). Western European beer volume fell 3.9% in H1 2026 and 4.2% in Q3.
  • China is cyclically weak and partly structurally weak. Chinese volume fell 6% in Q2 2026 and about 10% in Q3, the two quarters that carry two-thirds of China's profit. Peers show that part of the loss is share and channel rather than weather: Heineken's licensed volume through China Resources Beer grew in the mid-twenties per cent, and the on-premise share of Chinese beer has fallen from 51.5% in 2019 to 47.5%.
  • Mainstream competitors have turned to price in two markets, for rule-driven reasons that persist. In the UK, Heineken and Molson Coors cut alcohol strength and spent the duty saving on price. In Poland, Asahi has discounted through the disruption caused by the new deposit scheme.
  • Regulation is dense and sequenced against the company. Vietnamese excise rises about five points a year from 2027, the UK deposit scheme starts on 1 October 2027, and the UK sugar-tax threshold falls in January 2028.
  • Input costs turn against Carlsberg in 2027. Costs are neutral in 2026 under a 90% hedge, then a headwind of about 160bp of gross margin in 2027; oil at USD 111 makes the adverse tail fatter.

Carlsberg's tailwinds are real, but they are company-specific or mechanical, and none of them is a turn in demand. The tailwinds are PepsiCo's repeated choice of Carlsberg as its bottler (five markets in 2024, 17 by January 2029), alcohol-free beer (+11%), India (mid-teens volume growth, helped by the Karnataka excise reform), easy Chinese comparatives from Q2 2027, and a mild currency tailwind (+DKK 100m on 2026 EBIT).

The 2026 improvement in group volume came from a wider perimeter, not from consumers drinking more. Organic volume moved from -2.0% in FY2025 to +1.7% in H1 2026 and +0.3% in Q3, but the Kazakhstan licence added 1-1.5 points of that growth and laps in 2027. In the terms of Viewforth's "Use, Refill or Price" test, the lift came from the perimeter, not from use.

So what. The thesis has to rest on self-help, and the model should not lean on demand: it assumes underlying volume flat to +1%, and price and mix of 2-3% linked to local inflation. The macro backdrop is currently a valuation tailwind (a defensive rotation, with the US 10-year yield near 5.1%) and an earnings headwind (a squeeze on European discretionary spending and Chinese austerity). A valuation tailwind combined with an earnings headwind is a fragile combination.

Counter-case. Soft drinks (31% of volume, +8.5% in Q3), alcohol-free beer and India are growing categories that Carlsberg owns. Bernstein's framing (25% of volume with high intrinsic growth, 50% with moderate growth and 25% in structural decline) implies that steady low-single-digit volume growth is achievable. If Chinese inventories are clean (management says they were by end-September) and the summer of 2027 is normal, the easy comparatives alone add 1-2 points to Asian volume.

Against the market. The sell-side read Q3 as "multi-beverage validated", because soft drinks offset beer. I agree that the diversification works as a defence, but I give more weight than the sell-side does to the share-and-channel element of China's weakness and less to weather, and I count the Kazakhstan volume as perimeter, not demand. I agree with consensus that China's weakness in 2026 is partly weather and partly demand, and that 2027 gets the easy comparatives.

What would change my view. Chongqing Brewery's Q4 2026 volume no worse than -5%, with its margin flat in Q1 2027, would show that destocking is over and the Chinese weakness is not structural. Western European beer volume stabilising while price and mix holds above 2% would also change my view.

Conclusion: The operating environment is a moderate and worsening headwind, offset only by mechanical and company-specific tailwinds, so the investment case cannot rest on demand.

Score: 35, set by the Rater. External forces are a moderate and worsening net headwind: structurally flat-to-declining beer (footprint +0.3% a year, Western Europe -4%), a China slump that is partly share and channel loss, rule-driven mainstream price competition in the UK and Poland, sequenced regulation (Vietnam excise, UK deposit scheme, sugar) and a 2027 input-cost round of about 160bp, against only company-specific or mechanical offsets (PepsiCo choices, alcohol-free, India, easy China comparatives); consensus sales growth at the 31st percentile confirms no demand help. I agree with the group's 35 and place it just below Entra's mildly negative rate backdrop and above Vodafone's blocked price rises and mature-market decline.

#2Internally-driven corporate change forces, and the absence of problems

Internal change is the investment case, and the change is broad, resourced and largely delivered on the lines management controls. Since September 2023 the chief executive has:

  • launched the Accelerate SAIL strategy;
  • closed the DKK 29.5bn Britvic acquisition within 18 months, delivered about 30% of the synergies in year one against a plan of 10-15%, and raised the synergy target to GBP 110m (about 80% delivered by end-2026);
  • sold 25% of Southeast Asia to Sapporo at 21.3x 2025 EBIT, against a group multiple near 12x;
  • issued the hybrid bond to protect the BBB+ credit rating;
  • won three PepsiCo territories;
  • opened the USD 344m Kazakhstan plant on schedule on 1 October 2026;
  • rebuilt the Executive Committee (about 30% refreshed, with seats for marketing and IT and the return of the supply-chain chief); and
  • cut leverage from 3.9x to 3.0x in twelve months.

The change already shows in profit. Organic EBIT grew 5.0% in FY2025 on volume of -2.0%, and 5.9% in H1 2026 despite the Chinese floods. The chief executive bought DKK 1.69m of shares in September 2026 at DKK 845.

Three change forces still lie ahead, and they matter most for the next 18 months. First, the Kazakhstan margin step: toll-filling cost 40bp of the Central and Eastern Europe and India (CEEI) segment's margin in H1 2026, and in-housing adds about DKK 200m of EBIT in 2027 and DKK 100-150m in 2028. Second, the Azerbaijan licence, which starts on 1 January 2027 and breaks even in year one. Third, the buyback restart. The Indian listing is an option, not part of the base case.

The negatives are internal too, and four of them stand out.

Earnings quality is in transition. Special items were DKK 1.9bn in 2025, a 35% gap between adjusted and reported profit. The IFRS 18 restatement, the hybrid's place outside finance costs and minorities growing faster than EBIT all make reported earnings harder to read.

Returns fell with Britvic. Return on invested capital including goodwill fell from 13.8% in 2024 to 10.1% in 2025 (10.8% on a rolling basis at mid-2026). The initial post-tax return on Britvic is roughly 5-7% on the Analyst's estimate.

Working capital has quietly supported cash, and the support could reverse. Trade working capital weakened to -15.6% of revenue from -20.1% excluding Britvic, while supplier finance rose 20% to DKK 3.2bn, with payment terms of up to 180 days.

The culture is being rewired from cost-first to revenue-weighted incentives, with the bonus cap raised to 150% of salary. The new incentives are the mechanism by which the cost discipline the thesis relies on could erode. The observable tests are marketing spending above 8.5% of revenue and special items failing to narrow.

Finally, the revenue algorithm of 4-6% organic growth has never been met, as the chart shows.

So what. Credit the internal changes with 5-7% organic EBIT growth, about 30bp a year of margin gain, deleveraging to 2.5x by end-2026 and a buyback from mid-2027. Do not credit them with the revenue algorithm. Most of the profit effect is already in consensus. The three positives not yet priced are the buyback, any beat on FY2026 guidance (worth about 1% of EBIT against FactSet's consensus at the guidance midpoint, and about nil against Bloomberg's 5.8%), and Kazakhstan beating its plan.

Counter-case. Carlsberg's culture of under-promising is intact (Deutsche Bank: "Carlsberg don't do disappointments"), and employee engagement is 82/100. Today's executive team is deeper in supply chain, marketing and beverages than the team that ran the Funding the Journey programme; the finance director spent about 20 years at Diageo. If the growth culture adds a point to volume without losing cost discipline, management's informal ambition of "high-single-digit" EBIT growth is reachable.

Against the market. I am aligned with the market on the strength of execution, and I differ in two ways. First, I quantify the fade: self-help supplies more than half of FY2026-27 EBIT growth and about a sixth of FY2028's, and it turns negative in 2029 with the transition costs of the Nordic licence swap; no house articulates the fade. Second, I am more alert to the culture shift, which only Jefferies raises.

What would change my view. A new efficiency programme announced at a strategy cycle (likely by 2028) would extend the self-help runway. Two signals would say the growth culture is spending the savings: marketing stepping up to 9% of revenue at once (about DKK 650m, 4% of EBIT), or special items failing to narrow in FY2026.

Conclusion: Internal change is strong, resourced and reliably executed on profit, cash and the balance sheet, but its profit effect is largely in consensus and largely spent by end-2027, and the revenue line remains unproven.

Score: 64, set by the Rater. Broad, resourced and largely delivered self-help: Britvic closed and synergies ahead of plan (target raised to GBP 110m), the Sapporo stake sold at 21x EBIT, the Kazakhstan plant on time, leverage cut from 3.9x to 3.0x, a rebuilt Executive Committee and a buyback restart from mid-2027, supplying more than half of FY2026-27 EBIT growth and lifting EPS growth from about 3% to 8% a year; net of Britvic's sub-cost-of-capital return, unclean earnings, a culture shift that could spend the savings, a never-met revenue algorithm and a self-help runway that fades after 2027. Coherent with the group's 64: more earnings effect and proof than Teqnion's clean-up, less step-change than OEM's EQT-led acquisition drive.

#3Value chain, industry structure, business model, financial profile and management

Beer is a concentrated, rational oligopoly, and that structure supports price discipline at group level. The top five brewers hold 53% of global volume, and the top three earn 51% of beer EBIT. Private label is only about 9% of beverages, excise is passed through within months, and demand is inelastic (price elasticity of -0.30 to -0.47). Together these features make inflation-linked pricing credible.

Within the oligopoly, Carlsberg is the third of three, and the value chain presses on its volume. Carlsberg has about 5% of global beer volume, against 25% for AB InBev and 12% for Heineken. Carlsberg leads in only 24% of its own volume by weight and is a challenger in 66%; AB InBev leads in 75% of its own volume. Four pressures bear on Carlsberg's volume: consolidating European grocery retailers (Carlsberg suffered a 4-6 week delisting in Switzerland in Q4 2025); Heineken out-executing in Chinese and Vietnamese premium beer; AB InBev's BEES digital platform, which carries 73% of AB InBev's revenue, against Carlsberg's Servd platform, which is not yet monetised; and regulators adding excise, sugar and packaging costs.

Consolidation in beer favours AB InBev and Heineken, but Carlsberg is winning a different consolidation: PepsiCo bottling and multi-beverage distribution in Northern Europe and Central Asia. The PepsiCo volume comes at about a 20% discount to the group's price per hectolitre, which costs about 30bp a year of mix, but it lowers the cost of serving each outlet.

Carlsberg's competitive advantages are local and real, not global. Carlsberg is number one or two in 25 beer markets that carry about 70% of its volume: the Nordics, Switzerland, Western China, Laos, Central Vietnam, Kazakhstan, Ukraine, Malaysia and Singapore, with second place in India. The advantages rest on lock-in with bars and restaurants (through DraughtMaster dispense systems and trade loans) and on local density.

Profit sits where Carlsberg leads. Asia earns a 26.3% operating margin and an 81.8% return on invested capital excluding goodwill; Western Europe, where Carlsberg is mostly a challenger, earns 13.8%.

The multi-beverage advantage compounds, but licences can also be lost. Each new licence lowers the cost of serving the next, and the Nordic multi-beverage model has run above group margins for 25 years. Licences also move away: Carlsberg lost San Miguel in 2025 (2-3% of EBIT), and the Coca-Cola licence in Denmark and Finland ends in December 2028. The measurable scale penalty against AB InBev lies in cost of goods sold and EBITDA margin (table above), and marketing spending at 8.3% of revenue sits below the group's own 8.5-9% framework.

Carlsberg's financial profile is middling by absolute standards and leading within European brewers. Operating margin is about 15.6-15.8% (table above). Gross margin is 45-46%, against a 47-49% target that Carlsberg will not reach by 2028. Cash conversion is about 85-90% of adjusted net income and should improve towards 95-105% by 2028, as capex steps down from DKK 6.5bn and restructuring cash fades. Leverage is 3.0x and falling, and return on invested capital is 10-11% including goodwill. Trade working capital is a genuine outlier, at -17% of revenue on the company's measure, matching AB InBev.

EPS compounded at only about 3% a year over FY2019-25 on Viewforth's definition. Three drags held EPS back: Russia (the DKK 47.7bn seizure), the cost of financing Britvic (net interest rose from DKK 0.75bn to DKK 2.64bn) and special items.

Carlsberg's capacity to reinvest at high returns is limited, and that limit caps the fair multiple at the low-to-mid teens. Capex of 6-7% of revenue goes into PepsiCo plants, India and Vietnam; the business cannot reinvest 20% of sales at high returns, so the high-teens multiples of 2017-19 are not the right reference.

Management is a strength on the part of the case it controls. Guidance has been met or beaten at the top of the initial range nearly every year since 2016, and dated projects land on time. Capital allocation shows an instinct for arbitrage: Carlsberg sold the Sapporo stake at 21.3x EBIT, and bought the Indian minority for USD 744m in 2024 ahead of a float at Indian multiples (United Breweries trades near 60x earnings). Management has four weaknesses: Britvic was bought at 13.6x EBITDA and diluted returns; the revenue algorithm is undelivered; the senior team is small, with no visible successor to the finance director; and the culture is in transition.

Governance is prudent, inside an ownership structure that rules out a takeover premium. Six of the eight shareholder-elected directors are independent, and the audit is out to tender. The Carlsberg Foundation holds 30% of the capital and 77.5% of the votes. Foundation control rules out activism and any takeover premium, and it favours a progressive dividend and buybacks over radical change.

So what. Carlsberg is a medium-quality, low-cyclicality business run by a high-quality operator. It has predictable profit, nominal pricing power, local moats, a growing franchise-bottling business whose economics are set by PepsiCo's concentrate pricing, and returns diluted by one large deal. Carlsberg merits a multiple between Heineken's and AB InBev's, not AB InBev's.

Counter-case. Jefferies' critique carries some force. "Beyond beer" strategies have a mixed record (US hard seltzer), soft drinks are a lower-margin franchise business, and Carlsberg's footprint is "the narrowest and most concentrated" among global brewers. If the density gains from multi-beverage distribution do not show up in Western Europe's margin (13.2% in 2025, forecast at 14.2% in 2027), the strategy's premise weakens.

Against the market. I agree with the market that the business is medium quality and the operator high quality. The market under-weights two things: minorities (14.65% of profit and rising), which are a structural leak from the best regions, and the scale penalty in cost of goods sold. The market over-weights the multi-beverage advantage as a consumer moat. The advantage is a moat with retailers and outlets: durable in the relationship, but no protection against consumers trading down.

What would change my view. Western Europe's margin reaching 14.5% or more by FY2027, with soft-drink gross margin disclosed above 30%, would prove the density gains. In the other direction, Chongqing's mainstream brands losing share in Western China to China Resources Beer's pricing would show that the stronghold moat has been breached.

Conclusion: A rational industry and strong local positions support price discipline and predictable profit, but Carlsberg is a medium-quality challenger with nominal pricing power and diluted returns, run by a management that is excellent on profit and unproven on growth.

Score: 58, set by the Rater. A concentrated, rational beer oligopoly and real local number-one positions (70% of volume, Asia at a 26% margin) give price discipline and predictable, low-cyclicality profit under a high-quality operator, but Carlsberg is the third-placed challenger (leads in only 24% of volume) with nominal pricing power, a cost-of-goods scale penalty against AB InBev, minorities leaking 15% of profit from its best regions and new capital (Britvic) earning roughly 5-7%, below its cost. The figures agree with a middling profile (ROIC 8.2% at the 59th percentile, operating margin at the 52nd, ROE at the 81st only through leverage of 3.5x), consistent with groups of 60/56/45/68; it sits just below Indutrade's sound but flawed compounder and above Shell's cycle-bound returns.

#4Conservatism of guidance, proactivity with the sell-side, and the record of delivery and upgrades

Carlsberg's guidance pattern is consistent and well known: open with a wide range, narrow it upward at the half year, and deliver at or above the top. The initial range is about four points wide, and management narrowed it upward at the half year in 2023, 2024, 2025 and 2026 (chart below). For 2026, the range opened at 2-6%, was narrowed to 4-6% on 19 August and was repeated on 29 October; the model expects delivery of 5.5-6.0%. Jefferies counts beats against the initial midpoint of 300-870bp a year since 2016.

The size of the beat is shrinking: about 300bp in 2024, 200bp in 2025 and probably 150-200bp in 2026. A shrinking beat matters for upgrades, not for delivery.

Guidance is unusually specific in its building blocks and unusually silent on the lines that decide EPS. Management guides organic EBIT on a stated base, currency translation in kroner, net finance costs, tax, capex, leverage with a date, synergy phasing, the marketing ratio, the gross-margin target, and a split of growth into one-third volume and two-thirds price and mix. Management is silent on the four lines that decide the composition of EPS: price and mix by region, China's profit, minorities, and the treatment of the hybrid.

For FY2026, delivery at 6% is only a small beat, because consensus already sits near the top of the range. On the restated base, FactSet consensus EBIT of DKK 14,472m equals the guidance midpoint exactly (DKK 13,686m × 1.05 + DKK 100m of currency), while Deutsche Bank reports the Bloomberg consensus at 5.8% organic growth, near the top. Delivery at 6% is therefore a beat of about 1% against FactSet and about nil against Bloomberg. The guidance habit still protects against disappointment, but it no longer creates upgrades, because the sell-side has learned to sit at the top of the range.

Informal commentary sits above formal guidance. Management has spoken of "higher EBIT growth than 4-6%" (FY2025 results call), "compounding high-single-digit operating profit growth" (capital markets day, October 2025) and "growing confidence in MSD+ organic EBIT", meaning mid-single-digit growth or better (August 2026 roadshow). According to Bernstein (August 2026), the chief executive "firmly expected mid-single-digit EBIT growth" for 2027. Adjusted for the synergy tailwind (about 3 points of 2026 growth), FY2026 guidance implies only 1-3% underlying organic EBIT growth. That implied underlying rate is conservative relative to the help from synergies, and realistic given China and the Kazakhstan toll-filling losses.

So what. Treat profit guidance as a floor and timelines as reliable, and haircut the revenue ambition by 1-2 points. For 9 February 2027, expect an opening FY2027 range of 2-6% or 3-7%, with a midpoint of 4-5%, below consensus EBIT growth of 5.9% (about 70% probability). Expect a conservative finance-cost guide (DKK 1.5-1.7bn excluding currency), which is the one line likely to surprise the sell-side positively. Expect the upward narrowing in August 2027 (60-65% probability). The probability that FY2027 guidance is cut during 2027 is 10-15%, concentrated in a Chinese relapse combined with price missing costs; the probability that guidance is raised above its initial top is about 10%.

Counter-case. The consistency of the beat is itself the asset. A company that opens below what it expects to deliver gives forecasts a floor that most European companies do not. The sell-side also held its numbers through conservative openings in 2025 and 2026, so the February midpoint is a risk to sentiment, not to estimates.

Against the market. I am aligned with the market on conservatism, but I differ on the consequence. The market treats the habit as fuel for upgrades (Deutsche Bank forecasts 6.2% for FY2026, against consensus of 5.5-5.8%); I treat it as insurance on delivery that produces no upgrades. I also weight the February 2027 reaction (an opening below consensus plus the first clean IFRS 18 year) more heavily than any house does.

What would change my view. A FY2027 opening range of 4-7% or narrower would be a positive signal that management is breaking its own pattern. A midpoint below 4% would put the case into its downside scenario.

Conclusion: Guidance is conservative by a habit the sell-side has fully learned, so it underwrites delivery rather than upgrades, and the next opening, on 9 February 2027, is more likely to disappoint sentiment than to lift estimates.

Score: 72, set by the Rater. A decade-long record of wide, conservative profit ranges narrowed upward at the half year and delivered at or above the top (2024 1-5% to 6.0%, 2025 1-5% to 5.0%, 2026 2-6% to 4-6%, expected 5.5-6%) with dated projects on time, but the beat is shrinking and now sits at consensus, the 4-6% revenue target has never been met and the gross-margin target will be missed. Coherent with the guidance group's 68 lifted slightly for the length of the profit record; it sits just below Maersk's repeated low-set-and-raise pattern and above Linea Directa's honest-tracker record.

#5Pricing power, operating leverage, financial leverage, cost-out scope and feedback loops

Carlsberg's operating leverage is material on paper but managed in practice, so it shows up in gross margin and brand investment rather than in EBIT. About 35-40% of the cost base is fixed within a year. With costs flat, 1% of revenue moves EBIT by about 1.5%, and 1% of Western European volume is worth about DKK 220m of EBIT. The record shows management absorbing that leverage:

  • In 2020, organic revenue fell 8.4%, but EBIT fell only 3.1%, because marketing and administration costs were cut by 14%.
  • In 2022-23, cost of sales per hectolitre rose 13% and gross margin fell 290bp over two years, yet organic EBIT grew about 5% in 2023.
  • In 2025, volume fell 2% and EBIT grew 5%.

The leverage that matters for the forecasts is price against cost. A 1% move in price is worth about 6% of EBIT; a 1% move in volume is worth about 1.5-1.8%. Three pockets of genuine fixed-cost leverage do move the numbers. Chinese breweries are a drag in 2026 and turn positive on easy comparatives from Q2 2027 (Chongqing's Q3 showed volume -9.6%, gross margin -2.3 points and operating margin -2.5 points). The Kazakhstan plant gains as its utilisation builds in 2027-28. The Danish and Finnish production lines face a risk around the 2029 switch from Coca-Cola to PepsiCo; in the 2019 border-trade precedent, volume on the Danish canning lines fell 30%.

Financial leverage is elevated, falling and comfortable, but the hybrid coupon absorbs most of the interest saving. Leverage was 3.0x at H1 2026 and should be about 2.5x at end-2026. Fixed rates cover 84% of debt, and only DKK 472m of bonds mature within two years. A 1-point rise in interest rates costs DKK 98m a year, and refinancing at 6.5% would cost 1.1% of third-year EPS, the lowest sensitivity in Deutsche Bank's sector screen. Each DKK 5bn of debt repaid saves about DKK 175m of interest (+1.5% to EPS). Net of the hybrid coupon (insight 2), however, financing adds only about half a point to EPS growth in each of FY2026 and FY2027, and from 2028 the balance sheet's contribution to EPS runs through the share count.

The scope to cut costs is real and earmarked: about DKK 1.2-1.4bn of identifiable benefits over FY2026-28. The benefits are Britvic synergies (DKK 475m in 2026 and DKK 190m in 2027), Kazakhstan in-housing (DKK 200m in 2027 and DKK 100-150m in 2028), restructuring paybacks of about DKK 200-300m a year at run-rate, and about 1% a year of ongoing efficiency. About two-thirds of the benefits reach EBIT; the rest funds marketing (rising from 8.3% of revenue towards 8.5-9%) and price.

Peer experience warns against assuming more of the savings reach profit. Only about 25% of Heineken's EverGreen savings dropped through to profit. Carlsberg's own Funding the Journey programme (DKK 3bn of savings and +300bp of margin over 2015-19) started from a lower margin and was run by a cost-first culture, so its record is not a guide to today.

So what. Revenue growth of about 3% becomes EBIT growth of about 5% and EPS growth of about 8% through named cost actions, price covering cost in money and a falling share count, not through volume leverage. That translation is reliable in direction and modest in magnitude. Carlsberg has no self-accelerating case.

Counter-case. Redburn sees the UK margin rising from 12% to 15% by 2029 on density gains. DNB Carnegie puts each new mid-sized PepsiCo territory at +4-8% to EPS over time, and a Polish licence (which Jefferies calls "not guaranteed") would be a real reinforcing step. If utilisation in Kazakhstan reaches group margins in 2027 rather than 2028, operating leverage turns positive a year early.

Against the market. The market reads the cut in finance-cost guidance as a saving, and Morgan Stanley reads the Kazakhstan step as "a step-up to 10% organic EBIT growth in 2027". I read the finance-cost cut as largely reclassification plus coupon, and the Kazakhstan step as about DKK 200m, or 1.4 points of EBIT growth. The whole FY2027 EBIT increase of about DKK 730-790m breaks down as the chart below shows.

What would change my view. A CEEI margin above 18% in H1 2027, with Kazakhstan's soft-drink gross margin at Redburn's 35%, would prove the positive leverage. Marketing above 8.5% of revenue in FY2026 would show the savings are being spent.

Conclusion: Revenue growth turns into outsized profit growth here through price covering cost, named self-help and a falling share count, not through volume leverage or lower interest, so the amplification is real but modest and rate-limited.

Score: 58, set by the Rater. The structure has real but modest gearing: 35-40% of costs are fixed within a year, a 1% price move is worth about 6% of EBIT, DKK 1.2-1.4bn of cost-out is earmarked for FY2026-28 and a falling share count adds 2.5-3.5 points of EPS growth, so 3% revenue turns into about 8% EPS (about 2.7 times, above the Universe's typical 2 times). It stops well short of 75 because pricing power is nominal not real, operating leverage has historically been managed away through cost flexing rather than shown in EBIT, the hybrid coupon absorbs most of the interest saving, and the feedback loops are rate-limited by soft-drink mix and minority leakage; the groups' 45 and 44 read the financial profile, not this structural leverage.

#6Forecast financials; scope for double-digit growth; scope for higher growth and margins than the past

The model's forecasts (after update 2) compound EPS at about 8% a year on revenue growth of about 3%.

On the cleaner adjusted figures, EPS growth dips to about 5.5% in FY2027, the pinch year, and runs at 8-9% in every other year. The model's FY2026 EPS of DKK 64.50 blends the reported H1 2026 (after special items and purchase-price amortisation) with a forecast H2. The blend depresses FY2026 EPS by about DKK 1.8 and inflates FY2027 growth to +9.9%. The cross-check's DKK 66.30 is the cleaner adjusted figure, and on it the growth path is +9% (FY2026), +5.5% (FY2027), +9% (FY2028), +8% (FY2029) and +9% (FY2030).

The model sits 1-3% above the cross-check from FY2027 for a mechanical reason, not a judgement. The model retires shares at about today's price; the cross-check assumed rising prices of DKK 1,000-1,220.

Cash available to Carlsberg's shareholders is about DKK 2.5bn a year below FactSet's free-cash-flow line, because of leases, the hybrid coupon and dividends paid to minorities. The model's free cash flow (DKK 6.4bn rising to DKK 9.6bn) is after leases and before the hybrid coupon and minority dividends; the Analyst's own figure of DKK 7.2-11.2bn also adds back restructuring cash and dividends from associates.

Against consensus, the model matches in level but differs in route. The model has lower revenue and outer-year EBIT, cheaper financing, larger minorities and a buyback. The two-broker FY2029 EBIT of DKK 17,518m implies EBIT growth of 8% in 2029, which is too high.

EPS growth of about 8% a year is about three times the FY2019-25 rate, and the acceleration is credible because its sources are mechanical rather than heroic. Three drags stop (Russia, Britvic financing and special items), synergies are banked, and buybacks restart.

Double-digit EPS growth is the upside case, not the base. It needs India's listing proceeds spent on buybacks and DKK 4-5bn of buybacks every year from 2028; that combination is what Bernstein's 13% a year assumes. On margins, +140bp over five years is better than the past and worse than management's "high-single-digit" compounding. The 47-49% gross-margin target has about a 25% chance of being met by 2028 and a 50% chance of being dropped or pushed out.

The driver that decides FY2028-30 EPS, price over cost, is also the least certain one. The three largest positives in the FY2025-28 EPS gain of DKK 15.6 (price over cost, interest saved and synergies) supply about 100% of the net gain, as the chart shows. Two of the three, synergies and interest, are nearly settled; price over cost is diffuse.

Counter-case. Three things would lift the path: Deutsche Bank's 6.2% EBIT growth for FY2026; Bernstein's and DNB Carnegie's FY2027 EPS of about DKK 75, if their treatments of finance costs and minorities are right and the model's are wrong on both counts; and a new efficiency programme at a 2028 strategy cycle. Management's informal ambition of 7-9% EBIT growth a year is the upside case, giving FY2027 EPS of about DKK 72.5 and FY2028 EPS of about DKK 81.

Against the market. The model is at consensus in level. It is below consensus on revenue and on FY2028-29 EBIT, and above it on finance savings and the share count. I retire the previous memo's most likely path of 9.2% a year EPS growth (FY2027 DKK 70.7, FY2029 DKK 84.4), because that path needed revenue growth of 3.7% and EBITDA compounding at 5.6% after the synergies end.

What would change my view. Q1 2027 revenue per hectolitre above +3% (price running ahead of cost) would move me towards 6-7% EBIT growth; below +2% would move me towards 3%. A FY2027 finance-cost guide above DKK 1.8bn would take DKK 1-1.5 off the model's EPS.

Conclusion: The forecasts describe an 8%-a-year EPS compounder on 3% revenue growth and 5% EBIT growth, at consensus in level but not in composition. Double-digit growth is reachable only with India and a full buyback, and the higher-than-past growth and margins rest on self-help that is largely spent by end-2027.

Score: 60, set by the Rater. The growth sits in the upper part of the 5-10% band and the margin path (+140bp of EBIT margin to 2030 against a flat FY2019-25) is better than the past, but I place it mid-band rather than higher because much of it is financial and front-loaded (interest saved, the buyback, Britvic synergies from an acquisition) while the organic driver of FY2028-30, price over cost, is the diffuse one, and double-digit growth needs India and full buybacks; consistent with the forecasts group's 44 standing below the 11% Universe median.

#7Scope for upgrades to guidance, sell-side estimates and the narrative over 6-12 months

There is little scope for EPS upgrades either way, because consensus FY2027 EPS is already at the model's level. The corrections to consensus will come in parts, and in an unfavourable sequence: down first, up second.

Down first (to April 2027)

  • Revenue forecasts trimmed towards 3% (Jefferies 2.3%; Redburn cut to 3.0% on 29 October; FactSet sales revisions already -1% over twelve months).
  • The first full IFRS 18 year shows the hybrid coupon below net income: -DKK 1 to -3.6 a share at the brokers who have not deducted it.
  • Minorities raised at the brokers who forecast less than DKK 1,100m.
  • An opening FY2027 range with a midpoint below consensus.

Up second (February, then from August 2027)

  • A FY2027 finance-cost guide at or below DKK 1.6bn: +DKK 1-1.5 of EPS against brokers at DKK 1.8-1.9bn.
  • FY2026 delivered at about 6%, and leverage printed at about 2.5x.
  • From August 2027, the H1 beat, the upward narrowing and the buyback: +0.4% to FY2027 EPS and +2-3% to FY2028 as the lower share count enters brokers' models.

Net over 18 months, the changes to consensus EPS are small. FY2027 consensus moves by about nil to -2%, and FY2028 by -1% to +2%. FY2029 consensus (two brokers, still forming) is more likely to be raised by 2-4% once buybacks are modelled, provided FY2028 EBIT growth holds near 5%.

Guidance itself will follow its usual path: met for FY2026, opened conservatively for FY2027, narrowed upward in August 2027 and met again. Against the mid-term framework, Carlsberg will meet the leverage target a year early and keep its promise of "profit faster than revenue". It will miss the 4-6% revenue target again in 2026 and 2027 (about a 40% chance that the target is reset at the next strategy cycle), and it will not reach the gross-margin target. The informal "high-single-digit" compounding is the ambition most likely to be quietly dropped.

The sell-side knows the shape of the story but under-models its mechanics. Brokers cover the shape: synergies, Kazakhstan, the buyback's timing, whether China's weakness is weather or share loss, 2027 pricing, India, the Nordic switch and soft-drink mix. They under-model the mechanics: three houses miss the hybrid offset, minorities are modelled as a line but not at their true scale, and only one house addresses the shift in management incentives. The investor narrative is simpler, and bullish on the known parts (buyback coming, double-digit compounding). The market does not yet see two things: the pinch year, which is negative and arrives first, and the buyback's accretion, which is positive and arrives second.

So what. For an investor whose edge is being ahead of the sell-side, the window is the buyback, and it opens in August 2027. Over the coming 6-12 months, the scope for upgrades is nil at EPS, negative at revenue and positive at the share count, and the narrative is more likely to be surprised negatively in the spring than positively.

Counter-case. An Indian listing priced in December 2026 or January 2027 would bring DKK 4-5bn and could make a February buyback announcement plausible (about 15% probability now), reversing the sequence. India's market regulator, the Securities and Exchange Board of India, approved the pre-filing on 1 October, and the updated draft prospectus followed on 27 October. Deutsche Bank's upgrades after Q3 (+2.5% to FY2027-28 EPS, on currency) show that the houses still rating the shares Buy will use any reason to raise.

Against the market. The sell-side expects upgrades from the habitual beat; I expect the beat and no upgrades. The bull case's 13% EPS compounding is the one narrative item I expect to be marked down, not up, as investors read the February P&L.

What would change my view. An Indian listing with its proceeds committed to a buyback before February would change my view upward. A Chinese Q4 worse than -5% (in Chongqing Brewery's preliminary results in January) would change it downward, because the spring cuts would then reflect fundamentals rather than composition.

Conclusion: Upgrades over the next 6-12 months are unlikely at the EPS line and negative at the revenue line, and the one real upgrade (the share count) is dated to August 2027, so the narrative is likelier to deteriorate before it improves.

Score: 42, set by the Rater. At the EPS line consensus is already at the model's level, so the 6-12 month scope is about nil to slightly negative: a February opening range likely below consensus EBIT growth (about 70%), revenue trimmed towards 3%, the hybrid coupon and minorities forcing composition cuts first, with the finance-cost guide, the August narrowing and a buyback from August 2027 adding back +0.4% to FY2027 and +2-3% to FY2028 later in the window. Net FY2027 change of about nil to -2% against 3% revenue growth is a ratio a little below zero (around the 40th percentile), with the India listing a 15% upside option; coherent with the group's 46, placed just below Tele2's limited-further-raises case and above IMCD's limited scope on falling organic growth.

#8Current momentum in guidance, estimates, narrative, share price, and peers

Momentum is weak on both measures the framework rates: the dashboard grades sell-side momentum D and technical momentum D. Guidance momentum is positive but spent: management narrowed guidance upward on 19 August and repeated it on 29 October, raised the currency translation effect to +DKK 100m, and cut finance-cost guidance to DKK 1.8bn.

The sell-side composite masks a weaker component: EPS estimates have held up better than EBITDA estimates because finance-cost guidance was cut, partly through reclassification.

The six-month rise in the share price was the sector's, not the company's. About +10 points came from the sector (the October defensive rotation) and about -2 points from the company (the Q3 miss and the downgrades).

Investors in the sector are paying for volume momentum and buyback execution, not for cost-led stories with falling volume; Carlsberg sits between the two camps, as a cost-led story with a buyback coming. AB InBev is the sector's momentum stock, with consensus met or beaten in 15 of 17 quarters and a USD 6bn buyback running. Heineken has just posted volume growth of 3.9% against a consensus of 1.8%. Royal Unibrew shows what a lost licence does to a brewer's rating, and the spirits companies Diageo and Pernod Ricard trade at the 0th percentile of their own multiple ranges. The table compares the ratings.

So what. Momentum is more likely to worsen in the spring before it improves from August 2027. The buy share could fall into the low fifties if one or two of the remaining Buy ratings are cut on valuation after October's +14%. From August 2027, Carlsberg's sell-side momentum could move from D towards B, following the template AB InBev has set.

Counter-case. The dashboard rates Carlsberg A on its theme (defensive stocks in a risk-off market) and A on valuation (8th percentile). Bernstein raised its target to DKK 1,550 and Deutsche Bank raised its target by 3.4% after Q3, so the Buy camp is not capitulating. Read as a trend rather than as the last three months, the technical picture (price above a rising 200-day average) is better than the D rating suggests.

Against the market. I am aligned with the market, which also reads momentum as poor. I add the timing: momentum is likely to be worst at the February 2027 results and to improve thereafter.

What would change my view. Positive readings from Chongqing's Q4 results and from Heineken's Chinese business in January-February would change my view. So would the buy share falling below 50%, which would mark a clearing of sentiment that I do not currently see.

Conclusion: Momentum is weak on the sell-side and technically (D and D), the October rise was the sector's and not the company's, and the likelier path is deterioration into the spring and recovery from August 2027, on the template of AB InBev, the peer the market is paying for.

Score: 52, set by the Rater. The two measures split, so C; the parts confirm a weak C rather than moving the letter: guidance was narrowed up in August and repeated in October (positive but spent), FY2027 EPS revisions are 0% to -1% and EBITDA -2%, the buy share fell four points with a Jefferies downgrade, the narrative stalled on the Q3 volume miss, and the price sits above a rising 200-day average but fell 2% over three months after a sector-driven October rally. Peers are mixed (AB InBev strong, Heineken sell-side weak), so they neither lift nor lower it.

#9Riskiness and simplicity of the forecasts and expectations

The case is simple in direction and complex in composition. The 18-month EBIT range rests on four inputs: 2027 price and mix, China's Q2-Q3 2027 volume, the Kazakhstan step and the buyback date. Every other input moves EPS by less than about 1%. The complexity lies elsewhere: a wide perimeter (a commercial presence in more than 125 markets, production in about 30, two categories, and 17 PepsiCo markets by 2029); four unguided lines between EBIT and EPS; three reporting changes that hit comparability at once (IFRS 18 with the company's new performance measures, the hybrid's treatment as equity, and licence takeovers counted as organic growth); and a share price that answers to a sector multiple. Viewforth's Fitness for Fighting digest flags cases with many moving parts as a "Fragility Double Underweight", and the Carlsberg case qualifies.

The FY2027 EPS range is narrow and slightly skewed down. FY2027 EPS should land at about DKK 66.5-72.5 around DKK 70 (-5% to +3.5%), with about 25% probability below DKK 68, 55% between DKK 68 and 71.5, and 20% above. The expected value is about half a point below base. The skew is slightly negative because 2027 stacks a 160bp cost headwind, the Kazakhstan volume lap and the end of most synergies, with the negatives front-loaded in H1 and the positives back-loaded in H2. The FY2028 range is about DKK 70.5-81 around DKK 76.4, roughly symmetric.

Three features keep Carlsberg's earnings range narrow. The guidance culture makes outcomes one-sided against the initial midpoint; minorities stop half of any Asian swing from reaching EPS; and financing is fixed. The range is narrower than the sell-side's own FY2027 dispersion (±7%), and narrower than the ranges at Heineken (volume-led), Diageo (a price reset) or Royal Unibrew (a licence loss, a 240bp cost headwind and thin hedges).

The share-price range is wide, because the multiple's own five-year range runs from 9.95x to 18.83x. Over 18 months, the share-price range is -20% to +40% in the third forecast set's framing, and about -8% to +37% before dividends on the model's FY2029 EPS.

The case requires six things to hold.

  • Price covers more than 80% of input inflation in money, as it did in 2022-23 at the EBIT line, at a cost to gross margin.
  • Sapporo's purchase closes in Q4 2026; management has confirmed the timing.
  • Kazakhstan steps up within a year. A one-year ramp-up would be at the fast end of peer precedent: Royal Unibrew's Pepsi ramp-up and Coca-Cola Europacific Partners' German turnaround each took two to three years.
  • China gets its easy comparatives (a mechanical effect) rather than suffering structural share loss to Heineken through China Resources Beer in Western China (low probability, high impact).
  • Supplier finance (DKK 3.2bn) does not reverse.
  • The new culture does not spend the savings.

The sudden fundamental risks, in order of expected cost:

  1. A structural break in China: about -4% of EBIT for a 20% fall in Chinese profit, plus a delayed buyback.
  2. An energy and packaging shock: oil at USD 111 is already above the Fitness for Fighting digest's USD 100 trigger, Jefferies' stress case of USD 145 raises cost of goods sold by 25%, and the margin hit is 1-2 points if prices cannot follow.
  3. Political seizure or war: Russia's 2023 seizure is the precedent; Ukraine is about 3% of revenue; and the Kazakh and Laotian currencies cannot be hedged.
  4. A licence shock: very unlikely in the near term under ten-year rolling agreements, but losing San Miguel cost Carlsberg 2-3% of EBIT, and Royal Unibrew's licence loss cost it up to 23%.
  5. Regulatory escalation: an EU ban on alcohol advertising, or faster increases in Vietnamese excise.
  6. Legal claims at the associate Super Bock: a EUR 57m fine under appeal and private claims of up to EUR 467m, a tail risk to the associates line.

Sentiment risks are elevated, because the October rise was a sector rotation. The triggers are a reversal of the defensive bid (if the US 10-year yield falls below 4.5% or risk appetite returns); read-across from Heineken, China Resources Beer and Budweiser APAC, which report first; alcohol-health headlines; US tariff rhetoric, which took 2-4 points off the sector in April 2026; European sovereign stress; and further downgrades. A typical sentiment move is 5-15% without any change in fundamentals. Liquidity (USD 55-65m traded a day) is not a constraint.

The case is easy to track on what management controls and hard to track on what it does not. The profit floor, leverage and synergies are easy to follow. China's profit is never disclosed, so the quarterly filings of Chongqing Brewery and Carlsberg Malaysia, and peers' results, are the proxies. Price and mix is disclosed only at group level, and regional revenue per hectolitre at Q1 is the best proxy.

Beer is a low-cyclicality business, so the sector's precedents for underperformance are structural rather than cyclical. In 2020, Carlsberg's organic revenue fell 8.4% and EBIT only 3.1%, and the industry passes costs through within months. The precedents for underperformance are Heineken in 2019-25 (EPS +1.4% a year and a de-rating, as volume fell and the premium engine stalled), Diageo in 2023-26 (over-premiumisation, a price reset and a dividend cut) and Royal Unibrew in 2026 (a licence loss that took its multiple to the 1st percentile). Carlsberg carries some of Heineken's risk through China and mainstream beer, and none of the licence-loss risk in the near term.

The precedents for outperformance match Carlsberg's setup today, with one caveat. Carlsberg in 2015-19 and AB InBev in 2025-26 combined self-help, deleveraging and buybacks at a low multiple. The caveat comes from Carlsberg's own record: the company cancelled its 2020 buyback within weeks of launch when COVID hit, so a restarted buyback is not irreversible.

Downside case to hold in mind. Suppose Chinese volume is flat to down again in 2027, price and mix grows by less than 2% against input inflation above 5%, and the buyback slips to 2028. FY2027 EPS would then fall to about DKK 66.5-67 (5% below consensus) and FY2028 EPS to about DKK 70-71, and the shares would head towards a trough band of DKK 740-860 (a five-year 10th-percentile multiple on lower earnings). The 52-week low is DKK 729.

Counter-case. Against other listed European companies, Carlsberg's earnings predictability is in the top quartile: a management that manages to its number, fixed financing, no covenant or solvency question, and a dated catalyst. The complexity lies in presentation, and the February 2027 results resolve much of it.

Against the market. The market prices China as the main risk. I agree that China is the main share-price risk, and I add that its EPS effect is about half what the price reaction implies. The market under-prices the risk in the pinch year's composition, and it over-prices nothing in particular.

What would change my view. Three observations by mid-2027 would say the thesis has started to rely on strengths Carlsberg does not have: Q1 2027 revenue per hectolitre below +2%; a CEEI margin below 18% in H1 2027; and Chongqing's H1 2027 margin still falling with inventories normal. Each would take 1-3% off FY2027 EPS, and none would break FY2026.

Conclusion: The earnings are predictable (about ±5% on FY2027 EPS, slightly skewed down) and the business is low-cyclicality, but the case is complex in composition, hard to track where it matters most, and exposed to a share-price range, set by Chinese results and sector flows, that dwarfs its earnings range.

Score: 55, set by the Rater. Earnings are unusually predictable for the Universe (FY2027 EPS cone about -5% to +3.5%, slightly skewed down; low cyclicality, 84% fixed-rate debt, a management that manages to its number), but the case is complex in composition (four unguided lines below EBIT, three reporting changes, 125 markets), poorly trackable on China and price, leverage is still elevated (3.5x, worse than 80% of the Universe), and the share price swings 5-15% on Chinese prints and sector flows within a -20% to +40% cone. Between the two risk groups (42 and 60); it sits just below Shell's resilient but commodity-noisy range and above Nexans's lumpy, sudden project risks.

#10Where the stock is in its lifecycle

By the dashboard's rule, Carlsberg starts in the Bottoming phase. The two-year forward P/E is at the 8th percentile of ten years, sell-side and technical momentum are both D, the buy share is falling, EBITDA revisions are mildly negative, and estimates have not cleared.

Three things say the turn up has a date. The balance sheet is turning ahead of plan: leverage fell from 3.9x to 3.0x in a year and should be about 2.5x at end-2026. The profit lines are already in their delivery phase: guidance has been beaten every year since 2016, and organic EBIT grew 5.9% in H1 2026. The restart of capital returns is dated to August 2027, with an Indian listing as the accelerant.

The volume line is stalled, and it will stay stalled through the Kazakhstan lap in H1 2027. Ten-year organic revenue growth is 3.1%, the 4-6% target has never been met, and total volume fell 0.4% in Q3.

The market has begun to price the turn before the company has confirmed it. The multiple has moved from its two-year median of 11.9x to 12.9x, the 78th percentile of its own post-Britvic range, on the October rotation rather than on estimates. That early pricing is why the shares gave back 3% on the first volume miss.

So what. The honest description is "bottoming, with the turn up dated by the buyback": Carlsberg is turning up on the balance sheet and on profit, stalled on volume, and not yet broadening, since there is no demand inflection and no upgrades. The figure above sets out what would move the phase forward at each step. The risk of slipping back to "collapsing" is low, but the risk of the stall extending is real, at about 25%.

Counter-case. By the dashboard's valuation rating (A) and the AB InBev precedent (AB InBev's shares rose 27-35% in the twelve months after leverage fell below 3x and a buyback was announced), the stock may already be turning up, and the spring weakness may be the last chance to buy it while it is still bottoming.

Against the market. The market's October bid treated the stock as turning up; the fall after Q3 treated it as bottoming. On momentum and estimates I side with bottoming; on the balance sheet and the calendar I side with turning up. The gap between the two readings is nine months.

What would change my view. An Indian listing in December with its proceeds committed to a buyback would move the phase to turning up now. A Chinese Q4 worse than -5%, combined with a FY2027 guidance midpoint below 4%, would entrench bottoming into H2 2027.

Conclusion: The stock is bottoming by the dashboard's rule and by its momentum, with a turn up that is dated (August 2027) and already partly priced by the October rotation, so the phase is best read as "bottoming, turning up on schedule" rather than turning up now.

Score: 53, set by the Rater. I agree with the memo's 'bottoming, turning up on schedule': the balance sheet and profit lines are already turning (leverage to 2.5x a year early, profit guidance beaten) and the buyback dates the turn to August 2027, but volume is stalled, estimates are drifting down, the spring brings a likely sentiment disappointment first, and the October rotation has already priced part of the turn (the multiple at the 78th percentile of its two-year range). It sits just above Solid State's bottoming-to-turning with uncertain timing, because the turn here is dated, and below Indutrade, whose order intake already hints at the turn.

#11The fair multiple

Viewforth's guideline fair multiple for a Bottoming stock is 15.27x, about 18% above today's 12.9x. The guideline is the 30th percentile of the stock's own ten-year two-year-forward P/E. Today's multiple, on consensus EPS and the corrected model, is 12.9x at DKK 960.6 (about 12.5x at DKK 934.2). Today's multiple sits at the 8th percentile of ten years, the 36th percentile of five years and the 78th percentile of the last two years. The guideline therefore sits at roughly the five-year 70th percentile, well below the ten-year median; the second chart below places each figure on one scale.

My central fair multiple at end-2027 is about 14x, because the ten-year history belongs partly to a different company. In 2016-21 Carlsberg carried leverage of 1.2-2.3x, ran annual buybacks of DKK 3-4bn, had a Chinese business growing profit at double digits, had no soft-drink franchise business, and traded at 16-21x. The post-Britvic company differs on five counts:

  • leverage is held at about 2.2-2.5x by design (management calls 2.5x "fit for the future business", so leverage will not go lower);
  • minorities take 14.65% of profit, and the share is rising;
  • China carries 30% of beer volume, and its premium engine has stalled;
  • a third of volume is in bottling, with economics set by PepsiCo; and
  • revenue grows at about 3%.

Against peers, a Carlsberg with 8% EPS growth belongs between Heineken and AB InBev. AB InBev trades at 15.6x, with 11% EPS growth, a buyback running and sell-side momentum A. Heineken trades at 12.9x, with 7-8% EPS growth and a new chief executive. The European beverage sector averages about 12.7x. Carlsberg combines 8% EPS growth, a buyback from August 2027 and a profit record better than Heineken's. The central 14x is close to the five-year median of 13.8x, and to the multiple at which the shares traded through most of 2024-25, before the China downturn.

The guideline 15.27x is the reachable top of the range, and reaching it needs three things to coincide: the buyback announced, China's comparatives delivered with Chongqing's margin recovering, and the sector holding its defensive rating. The floor is the five-year 10th percentile of 11.3x, which the stock visited in 2024-25; the spirits names show that the market leaves cost-led stories with falling volume at that level.

The guideline deserves less than full weight, because about two-thirds of the multiple's level is set by the sector (insight 7), and the sector is at decade lows for reasons the company cannot address: moderation in drinking, weight-loss drugs, Chinese consumption, tariffs and bond yields. A re-rating to 15.27x needs the sector to hold its October rating and the company to close its roughly 17% discount to peers. The company-driven half of that discount, worth 8-10% on the price, is what the buyback and a Chinese stabilisation can deliver.

The guideline deserves no further discount, because brewers do re-rate when deleveraging unlocks buybacks. Carlsberg re-rated to 18.7x in 2017-19, and AB InBev re-rated from the bottom of its range in 2025-26. The guideline of 15.27x is only the five-year 70th percentile.

Against the market. The sell-side's targets imply 14-15x on FY2027-28 earnings: a median of DKK 1,050; Morgan Stanley DKK 1,075, on a 16.5x twelve-month multiple that uses a different basis; Redburn DKK 1,100; and Bernstein DKK 1,550, on 13% compounding. My 14x sits at the conservative end of the sell-side and 1.3 turns below the guideline. The guideline is my upside, not my base.

What would change my view. A buyback of DKK 4bn or more announced with the H1 2027 results, plus two quarters of Chinese volume growth, would move my central multiple to 15x. A FY2027 guidance midpoint below 4%, with price missing costs, would move it to 12.5-13x.

Conclusion: The guideline fair multiple of 15.27x is a reachable upside for a stock turning up on its balance sheet, but the post-Britvic company's leverage, minorities, China weight and 3% revenue growth argue for a central fair multiple of about 14x at end-2027, and the sector will decide two-thirds of wherever the multiple lands.

Score: 77, set by the Rater. Cheap on one measure and neutral on the other gives B. I place it low in the band because part of the cheapness is deserved: the ten-year history belongs partly to a different company (lower leverage, double-digit China growth, no franchise bottling, fewer minorities), the stock is already at the 78th percentile of its post-Britvic two-year range and about two-thirds of the multiple is a sector call, so the memo's central fair multiple of about 14x is only about 12% above today's 12.5x.

#12Total shareholder return, by the DuPont split

At the guideline multiple, the model returns +40% over the 18-month column and +62.5% over three years, from DKK 960.6 on 28 October. Two-year-forward EPS today is about DKK 74.5 (12.9x). At 31 December 2027 the two-year-forward EPS is FY2029's DKK 83.77, and at 30 June 2029 it is the model's extrapolation of about DKK 96. The earnings and multiple parts multiply to give the share price, and dividends add to it.

Earnings. The 18-month earnings leg is about 13%, because the forward window rolls from a blend of FY2027 and FY2028 onto FY2029, picking up the recovery from the pinch year and the first full year of buybacks. The three-year earnings leg is about 29%, because the window rolls onto FY2030-31 and adds two more years of 8-9% compounding, with the share count falling 2.5-3.5% a year. Of the FY2025-29 EPS growth, about a third comes from Britvic synergies and Kazakhstan, about a third from net financing (interest saved less the hybrid coupon) plus the buyback, and about a third from price over cost; China is a round trip, and minorities are a drag.

Dividends. A payout of 48-50%, growing with EPS, gives a 3.4% yield today and adds about 7% of value over the 18-month column, which counts both the FY2026 and the FY2027 dividends.

The multiple. The multiple is the single largest part of the 18-month return and about 30% of the three-year return, and it is the part the company least controls.

The return at other multiples, from DKK 960.6 (add about three points for today's DKK 934.2)

How to read the return. The company-controlled return (earnings plus dividends, with no re-rating) is about 13% a year over the three-year column and about 17% annualised over the 18-month column; the 18-month figure is flattered by the roll onto FY2029, and in steady state the company-controlled return is about 12% a year. It rests on the predictable parts of the case: 5% EBIT growth, which management has delivered every year since 2016, a 3.4% yield, and a buyback from August 2027. A 12-13% controlled return is a good return for a defensive stock at the 8th percentile of its multiple, and it is why the downside at a trough multiple is a low-single-digit loss over 18 months rather than a large one. The re-rating leg adds 10-20 points over 18 months, depending on whether the multiple settles at my 14x or at the guideline 15.27x, and it is as much a sector call as a company call.
The probability-weighted 18-month return is about +22% including dividends, or around +19% annualised. The weights are 25% on the downside path (FY2029 EPS of about DKK 76 at 11.3-12x), 55% on the base (DKK 83.77 at 13-14x) and 20% on the upside (DKK 86-88 at 15.27x); the chart in the summary shows each case. The most likely outcome sits slightly below the mean, because the upside tail is fatter than the downside tail.

Against the market. The sell-side's median target (+12%) implies roughly 14x on FY2028 EPS over twelve months, consistent with my central multiple; Bernstein's DKK 1,550 needs 13% EPS compounding and a mid-teens multiple together. I expect the market to pay for the earnings leg from August 2027 and to argue about the multiple leg throughout.

What would change my view. A buyback larger than DKK 2bn in August 2027, funded by an Indian listing, would lift the earnings leg by 2 points a year. A sector de-rating on falling bond yields or tariff headlines would take the multiple leg to zero, regardless of delivery.

Conclusion: At the guideline multiple the model's return is +40% over the 18-month column (+33% annualised) and +62.5% over three years (+20% annualised). About 12-13% a year of that return (17% annualised over the short column) is earnings and dividends the company controls; the rest is a re-rating from 12.9x to 15.27x, which I would set centrally at 14x and which the sector will half decide.

Score: 78, set by the Rater. The weighted 18-month return falls in the 20-35% band, at about 77-80 on the scale. I hold it at 78 rather than higher because the lower tail is thin (about -4% to -8% at a trough multiple on downside EPS) and the upside tail fatter, but the mode sits below the mean, the 18-month column is flattered by rolling onto FY2029, and the near-term sequence (February-April 2027) runs against an investor entering now.

#13Summary conclusion on the business and its investment case

Carlsberg is a medium-quality, low-cyclicality beverage company run by a management that keeps its profit promises and has not yet kept its growth promise. The investment case is a self-help and capital-return compounder. Its earnings are unusually predictable, its earnings composition is unusually messy, and its share price answers to China and sector flows far more than to the P&L.

The sequence over the next 18 months is unfavourable first and favourable second. February to April 2027 brings a conservative guidance opening, the first clean IFRS 18 year showing the hybrid coupon, revenue forecasts cut towards 3% and sell-side breadth at its worst. August 2027 brings the H1 beat, the upward narrowing of guidance and the buyback. The entry is therefore more favourable after the spring corrections than before them, unless India's listing lands in December and brings the buyback forward.

The four memo ratings

CThesis's Change Forces' Strength: C. The internal forces are strong, broad and reliably executed, but they are largely in consensus and largely spent by end-2027; the external forces are a moderate headwind, and there is no demand inflection. The one force not yet priced is a dated buyback.
Thesis's Change Forces' Strength: 53, set by the Rater. Strong, delivered internal change (64) and real if modest leverage through cost-out, price over cost and the buyback (58) lift EPS growth from about 3% to 8% a year (C on topic 6), which just outweighs a moderate external headwind (35); the net change is mildly positive rather than material because the self-help fades after 2027, growth stays below the Universe median and there is no demand inflection.
CFoundations' Robustness: C. Profit delivery, cash conversion and the balance-sheet path are top-quartile. But earnings quality is in transition, Britvic diluted returns, pricing power is nominal, China is a fifth of profit with its premium engine stalled, and the revenue algorithm has never been met.
Foundations' Robustness: 63, set by the Rater. A rational oligopoly, strong local positions, low cyclicality and a decade-long record of profit delivery (topic 4 at 72) make the business more robust than its middling quality score (58) alone suggests, but the foundations stop well short of high because Carlsberg is a third-placed challenger with nominal pricing power, Britvic capital earning below its cost, rising minorities and a revenue algorithm never met.
BSetups' Fit/Crispness: B. The case fits the setup "Major Cause-for-Concern Clearing in a medium-quality non-cyclical business on a first-quartile multiple, leading to reversion to normal" cleanly on the balance sheet: leverage reaches 2.5x a year early, the buyback is dated, and the multiple is at the 8th percentile of ten years. The fit is less clean on the second cause for concern, China and volume, which is not clearing and keeps the reversion partial and dependent on the sector.
Setups' Fit/Crispness: 64, set by the Rater. The deleveraging a year early, a dated buyback and a bottom-decile own multiple fit the cause-for-concern clearing to reversion setup cleanly on the balance-sheet leg, but the second concern (China and volume) is not clearing and the reversion is partly a sector call, so the fit is good rather than crisp, in line with the memo's B.
CCase Riskiness: C. Earnings risk is low: the FY2027 EPS range is about ±5%, there is no solvency question, and management manages to its number. But the case is complex below EBIT, hard to track on China and price, and exposed to a share-price range, set by sector flows and Chinese results, that is three to four times its earnings range. The February 2027 results will resolve the complexity of the composition, not the exposure.
Case Riskiness: 54, set by the Rater. Low earnings risk (a narrow, slightly negative-skewed FY2027 cone, no solvency question, a management that manages to its number) is offset by complexity below EBIT, poor trackability on China and price, still-elevated leverage and a share-price cone three to four times the earnings cone, so the case sits a little above typical, coherent with topic 9 at 55.

End notes

Bases used throughout

"EBIT" is operating profit on Carlsberg's own performance measures (CPM; FY2025 base DKK 13,686m), the basis of guidance and consensus. "EPS" is the company's adjusted EPS (FY2025 DKK 60.81). "Leverage" is the company's net interest-bearing debt to EBITDA, which includes leases and half of the EUR 1.8bn hybrid bond. Money is in Danish kroner (DKK), and consensus is shown by named financial year.

The forecasts are the Financial Analyst's model after update 2. Update 2 deducts minority interests through the net-financial-items line, because the model has no minority line of its own; the model's row "net income before minority interests" is therefore after minorities in substance.

Prices and dates

The share price is DKK 934.2 at 29 October 2026. The model ran at DKK 960.6 (28 October), so the memo quotes returns at that price; at today's price every return is about three percentage points better.

Two cautions on the source files

First, the latest Earnings Review covers the Q3 2026 trading statement, which is newer than the H1 2026 results that FactSet shows as the last reported period; the Earnings Review is current and is used. Second, the dashboard's Phases page quotes today's two-year-forward P/E as 11.4x, a figure computed on the model's EPS before the minorities correction. On consensus EPS and the corrected model, the multiple is 12.9x at DKK 960.6 and about 12.5x at DKK 934.2. Every multiple in this memo uses the corrected figure, so the guideline fair multiple of 15.27x sits about 18-22% above today's multiple, not the 34% the Phases page shows.

The previous memo's return, and why it is replaced

The earlier model (before update 2) showed returns of +58% and +82% on EPS that was 13-16% too high, because minorities were never deducted. The earlier memo's most likely path of 9.2% a year EPS growth needed revenue growth of 3.7%. Both are retired. The dashboard's pin of C on total shareholder return and valuation reflected that disagreement; on the corrected figures, the return at the guideline multiple is strong and the return at an unchanged multiple is adequate.

Frameworks and abbreviations

The Universe is Viewforth's universe of covered stocks, against which percentiles and scores are set. The lifecycle phases (Collapsing, Bottoming, Turning up, Thesis broadening, Reinforcing) follow the Master Dashboard's Phase rule. The "Use, Refill or Price" test asks whether volume growth comes from consumers using more, from restocking or a wider perimeter, or from price. The Fitness for Fighting digest is Viewforth's guide to case fragility. Insight 7's finding that the sector sets about two-thirds of the multiple is the Analyst's reference D-07. CEEI is Carlsberg's Central and Eastern Europe and India segment. CPM is Carlsberg's own performance measures. ROIC is return on invested capital. TSR is total shareholder return.

Visuals

Default visuals (charts, images and tables) come from the Viewforth default-visuals set of 4 November 2026, built from the Financial Analyst's model after update 2, FactSet and the Master Dashboard. Charts in visuals/drawn were drawn for this memo from figures stated in the text; where a value is derived rather than stated, the note under the chart says so. The two charts in visuals/drawn-copy-editor (the sized judgements and the probability-weighted return) were drawn in the copy edit from figures stated in the memo, and their notes say which values are derived.
